alternatives.explanation: Confounding by planned slack. Late-receipt jobs may be ones that were already tightly scheduled (PO due date close to the customer promise date). If so, the 'ninefold' comparison, which matches on year, family, PO count, operation count and estimated hours but not on slack, credits late receipts with lateness that tight scheduling would cause anyway.
alternatives.test: Compare late-receipt and on-time jobs within the same planned slack (promise date minus the last PO due date), first in non-spike years and then matched on year x planned-slack week (capped at 6+ weeks) over all years. Then recompute the ratio and the excess late shipments.
alternatives.result: Late receipts are concentrated in tightly planned jobs. In non-spike years, 0.5129 of late-receipt jobs had planned slack of 14 days or less, against 0.1766 of on-time jobs (q364, q367). Within those slack bands the effect is real but much smaller. With 14 days or less of slack: late receipt 0.5471 (1,453 jobs) vs on time 0.0869 (10,234). With 15-21 days: 0.0984 (549) vs 0.0001 (15,752). With more than 28 days: 0.0026 (380) vs 0.0012 (20,359) (q364). Matched on year x slack week (all 3,524 late-receipt jobs matched): 0.3573 vs 0.1263, a ratio of 2.83 rather than 8.96 (0.3575/0.0399). The excess is 814 late shipments over 10 years, 81.4 a year, rather than 111.9 (q366, q367).

alternatives.explanation: Definition: 'material on time' means on time against the PO due date, not on time for the job. If vendors quoted longer lead times in 2021, material could be on time by the PO yet arrive later relative to the job. Job release is gated on material, so that time lands in create-to-release, which F8's 'release-to-completion' measure leaves out.
alternatives.test: Check whether job release equals the last receipt date. Track vendor lead (due minus ordered) and create-to-release by year and month. Correlate the monthly late rate of on-time-material jobs with create-to-release, PO lead and release-to-completion. Then decompose the 2021 excess into slack-at-release mix and within-slack rate.
alternatives.result: Release equals the last receipt date on 0.9953-1.0 of jobs with a receipt, and no job is released before its last receipt (q352). PO lead (due minus ordered) roughly doubled in 2021: steel 5.6 calendar days against 3.2-3.7 in other years, aluminium 13.9 against 6.7-7.3, stainless 12.2 against 6.0-7.7 (q357). Create-to-release averaged 9.1 days in 2021 against 5.5-6.2 in other years, and average slack at release fell to 23.8 from 26.4-27.6 (q344). In Apr-Oct 2021 it ran 8.0-9.4, while release-to-completion was back to 12.6-13.3 by Aug-Oct with late rates still 0.147-0.169 (q348). Across 120 months, the late rate of on-time-material jobs correlates 0.648 with create-to-release, 0.663 with PO lead and 0.493 with release-to-completion (q356). In 2021, 0.1921 of on-time-material jobs were released with 14 days or less of slack, against 0.1 in other years and in 2016 (q362). The 2021 late rate was 0.1593 against 0.0159 in other years. With other years' slack mix it would have been 0.1028, so about 0.394 of the excess comes from tighter slack at release and about 0.606 from higher late rates within the same slack (q362, q367; one ordering of a non-additive decomposition). In 2016 the slack mix was normal and the excess is all within-slack. So 2016 was an in-plant problem, while about four tenths of 2021 was longer material lead time that the late-receipt flag cannot see.

alternatives.explanation: Release-to-completion may be a trend rather than a spike signal, so slow flow may not explain lateness.
alternatives.test: Look at release-to-completion by year and month next to the late rate.
alternatives.result: This partly undercuts the throughput reading. Release-to-completion fell over the decade, from 21.4 days (2016) to 8.6 (2025). 2017 ran at 18.4 days, close to 2021's 17.2, yet had a late rate of only 0.0307 (q344). In early 2017 it was 18.2-20.7 days a month with late rates of 0.009-0.032 (q348). Still, at the same slack at release, both spike years were far worse than other years: with 15-21 days of slack, 0.0623 (2016) and 0.0281 (2021) against 0.0007, and with more than 35 days, 0.1842 and 0.0627 against 0.0039 (q360). An in-plant or shipping-side problem in both spikes survives. That release-to-completion time is its measure does not.

alternatives.explanation: Missing data: receipts are not recorded uniformly, so 'no late receipt' partly means 'no receipt recorded'.
alternatives.test: Look at unreceived PO share by year and vendor, and late rates for jobs with unreceived POs or outside-processing POs.
alternatives.result: The unreceived share is flat by year at 0.2884-0.3115 (q337), but it sits almost entirely with particular vendors. Vendor 1 (steel) has 0.4416 unreceived, vendor 2 (steel) 0.0011, aluminium 0.3881, stainless 0.4274, and the two outside-processing vendors 1.0 (q338). Jobs with an unreceived PO and no recorded late receipt ran late 0.0521 of the time, against 0.0331 for fully received on-time jobs (q336). Outside-processing jobs can never be flagged late-receipt. They ran late 0.6602 (206 jobs, 2016) and 0.6807 (119, 2021), and were 0.1375 and 0.0583 of all late shipments (q341). Because missingness is flat by year it does not create the spikes. But the late-receipt effect is measured only where receipts are recorded, and outside-vendor timeliness cannot be measured at all.

alternatives.test: Check the date ranges and the jobs that have no POs.
alternatives.result: POs and receipts start 2016-01-05, while job releases start 2015-11-27 (q335). 428 order jobs, all promised in 2016, have no PO at all and ran late 0.1262 of the time (q336). They are counted as 'no late receipt'. Jan 2016 shows 1 late-receipt job and a 0.141 late rate (q308, cited). This slightly inflates 2016's no-late-receipt rate. It does not affect the Sep-Dec 2016 spike.

alternatives.explanation: Seasonality: Sep-Dec or Mar-Oct may be late every year.
alternatives.test: Look at monthly late rates in non-spike years.
alternatives.result: No calendar month in non-spike years averages above 0.0379, and no single month-year above 0.0799 (q368). The spikes are periods, not seasons.

what_changed: (1) The per-job effect is overstated. Late-receipt jobs are disproportionately the tightly planned ones (0.5129 vs 0.1766 with 14 days or less between PO due date and promise date). Matched on year and planned slack, late-receipt jobs ship late 2.83 times as often (0.3573 vs 0.1263), not about nine times. The recoverable excess is about 81.4 late shipments a year, not 111.9 (q364, q366, q367). (2) 'The spikes came from jobs whose material arrived on time' needs heavy qualification for 2021. Release is gated on the last receipt (q352). Vendor lead times roughly doubled in 2021 (q357) and create-to-release rose to 9.1 days (q344). About 0.394 of the 2021 excess among on-time-material jobs is explained by tighter slack at release (q362, q367). Material lead time is part of the 2021 story, even though PO-due-date lateness is not. 2016 shows no such shift. (3) Release-to-completion time is weak evidence of slow flow. 2017 matched 2021 on that measure and had 0.0307 late (q344). The in-plant or post-release component is better shown by higher late rates at the same slack at release (q360). (4) Receipt recording is very uneven by vendor (q338), and outside processing is unmeasurable. The late-receipt effect applies only to recorded receipts. Not re-tested: the clocked-hours correlations (q298, q302) and segment breadth (q325). I accept them as cited, with the analyst's own caveat that labour work_date is posting-dated.
revised_conclusion: Observed: material received after its PO due date is associated with late shipment. Compared at the same year and the same planned slack (promise date minus PO due date), late-receipt jobs shipped late 0.3573 vs 0.1263 (2.83x; 3,524 jobs, promised 2016-2025), about 81.4 extra late shipments a year (q366). Most of that sits in jobs with 14 days or less of planned slack (q364). Late receipts were flat across years and do not explain the 2016 and 2021 spikes, which are periods rather than seasons (q368). The two spikes differ. In 2016 slack at release was normal, and jobs ran late far more often at every level of slack (q360, q362): the delay arose after material arrived (in-plant or before shipping). In 2021, vendor PO lead times roughly doubled (q357). Release, which waits for the last receipt (q352), slipped to 9.1 days after job creation (q344), and about four tenths of the 2021 excess is explained by the resulting tighter slack at release. The remaining six tenths is, as in 2016, higher lateness at the same slack (q362, q367). Interpretation: 2021 was partly a material-supply problem hidden by measuring receipts against PO due dates that had themselves been pushed out, and partly a post-release problem. 2016 was a post-release problem. For action: measure material timeliness against the job's need date, not only the PO due date. Protect slack on tightly planned jobs. Investigate post-release flow in Sep-Dec 2016 and Mar-Oct 2021.
not_evidence_of: Not evidence that late receipts cause the late shipments ninefold, or that 112 a year are recoverable. Even the slack-matched 81.4 a year is an association: rushed orders could produce both short PO due dates and late vendors. Not evidence that 2021 material supply was fine: 'on time' was measured against lengthened due dates. Not evidence of which work centre slowed. Operations carry only completion dates, and release-to-completion moved over the decade without tracking lateness (2017). Not evidence about vendors whose receipts are often unrecorded (vendor 1, aluminium, stainless) or about outside processors, which have no receipts at all. Not evidence that capacity was adequate: clocked hours are posting-dated, and I did not re-test them. No dollar figure is supported.
